title: Food, Shopping & Health
summary: Survival Korean for ordering and paying at restaurants, getting medicine at a pharmacy or clinic, and handling parcels and daily weather.

units.title: Ordering & Paying Out
units.situation: You sit down at a small Korean restaurant or step up to a cafe counter. There may be no English menu, and you need to call the staff over, order, and pay by card.
units.goal: Call a server, order food or drinks, ask if you can pay by card, and request takeout — using polite 해요체.

keyPhrases.note: The standard way to call staff in a Korean restaurant. Say it clearly, not too loudly. 저기요 works the same way.
Point at the menu or a dish while you say it. 이거 = this thing. Works for almost any item.
Water and side dishes (반찬) are usually free and self-serve, but it's fine to ask. 주세요 = please give me.
메뉴판 = the physical menu. Useful when only a wall menu is posted.

keyPhrases.en: Please ring me up. / The bill, please.
keyPhrases.note: In Korea you usually pay at the front counter, not at the table. 계산 = payment/calculation.
Almost everywhere takes card, but tiny shops or street stalls may be cash only. 돼요? = is it okay / does it work?

keyPhrases.en: To go, please. / Please pack it up.
keyPhrases.note: 포장 = packaging. For takeout. To eat in, say 여기서 먹을게요 (I'll eat here).

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Excuse me! Can I get a menu?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sure, here you go. What can I get you?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: This one, please. And some water.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Okay, one moment.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Excuse me, I'd like to pay. Do you take card?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.ko: 네, 카드 돼요. 여기서 찍어 주세요.
dialogue.en: Yes, card is fine. Please tap here.

beginnerGuide.title: 주세요 is your power phrase
beginnerGuide.body: Attach 주세요 (please give me) to almost any noun to order it: 물 주세요, 김치 주세요, 이거 주세요. To ask someone to DO something for you, use the verb stem + 아/어 주세요, as in 포장해 주세요 (please pack it) or 계산해 주세요 (please ring me up).

beginnerGuide.title: Calling staff is expected
beginnerGuide.body: It is completely normal and polite to call out 여기요! or 저기요! to get a server's attention — they will not come unless you do. Make eye contact, say it once, and wait. You do not need to raise your hand awkwardly or wait to be noticed.

beginnerGuide.title: You usually pay at the counter
beginnerGuide.body: In most Korean eateries you bring the bill (or just walk) to the front register to pay, rather than paying at your table. Card is accepted nearly everywhere; carry a little cash for small or older shops that may be cash only.

checkpoints: Call a server's attention with 여기요 or 저기요 without hesitating.
Order at least two items using 이거 주세요 and 물 주세요.
Ask whether card is accepted with 카드 돼요? and request the bill with 계산해 주세요.
Choose correctly between eating in (여기서 먹을게요) and takeout (포장해 주세요).

drills.note: Swap 이거 for any noun: 물 / 김치 / 커피 주세요.
Contrast with 여기서 먹을게요 = I'll eat here.
Reuse 돼요? for other yes/no checks: 여기 돼요? (is here okay?).

steps: Enter and seat yourself, or wait briefly if a sign says 안내 (you'll be seated).
Call the server: 여기요! and ask for the menu: 메뉴판 주세요.
Point and order: 이거 주세요. Add drinks/water: 물 주세요.
When finished, go to the counter: 계산해 주세요, then 카드 돼요?
For leftovers or takeout, say 포장해 주세요.

deepLinks.label: Find restaurants near you (Naver Map)
deepLinks.note: Search a dish or 맛집 (good restaurant) plus your neighborhood to see reviews, hours, and whether they do takeout.

units.costs: A casual single-dish meal (kimbap, noodles, rice bowl) typically runs about 6,000–10,000 KRW. Cafe drinks are roughly 3,000–6,000 KRW. No tipping is expected anywhere in Korea.
units.notes: Side dishes (반찬) and water are usually free and often self-serve — look for a water/utensil station near the entrance.

units.title: Pharmacy & Clinic
units.situation: You feel sick or have a headache. You need to describe what hurts at a clinic (병원), pick up medicine (약), and find or use a pharmacy (약국) — possibly with a prescription (처방전).
units.goal: Say where it hurts, find a pharmacy, hand over or ask for a prescription, and ask how to take your medicine — using 해요체 and want/must forms.

keyPhrases.note: The core word for feeling unwell or being in pain. Use it alone or with a body part: 머리가 아파요.
What staff will ask you. 어디 = where, 가 marks the subject (the part that hurts).

keyPhrases.en: My head hurts. / I have a headache.
keyPhrases.note: Swap the body part: 배가 아파요 (stomach), 목이 아파요 (throat). 가/이 marks what hurts.
Common cold symptom. 콧물 = nasal mucus, 나요 = it comes out. Also 기침이 나요 (I have a cough).
약국 = pharmacy, marked by 이. Pharmacies show a green cross sign. 약 alone = medicine.

keyPhrases.en: May I have the prescription, please.
keyPhrases.note: 처방전 = prescription slip. The clinic gives you this to take to a separate pharmacy.

keyPhrases.en: How do I take this medicine?
keyPhrases.note: 어떻게 = how, 먹어요 = take/eat. Koreans say 약을 먹다 (eat medicine) for taking pills.
V + 고 싶어요 = want to. For over-the-counter remedies you can buy directly at the 약국 without a 처방전.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.en: Where does it hurt?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: My head hurts. And I have a runny nose.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.en: It's a cold. I'll give you a prescription.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Thank you. Where is a pharmacy?

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.en: Your prescription, please. Here's your medicine.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: How do I take this medicine?

dialogue.speaker: Pharmacist
dialogue.en: Three times a day, after meals.

beginnerGuide.title: Clinic first, pharmacy second
beginnerGuide.body: In Korea, the doctor (병원/의원) diagnoses you and prints a 처방전 (prescription), but does NOT give you the pills. You take that slip to a nearby 약국 (pharmacy) — almost always within a short walk — to actually receive your medicine. For minor issues like a headache or cold, you can skip the clinic and buy over-the-counter medicine straight from the pharmacy.

beginnerGuide.title: Describe symptoms with [part]가/이 아파요
beginnerGuide.body: Name the body part, add 가 or 이, then 아파요: 머리가 아파요 (head), 배가 아파요 (stomach), 목이 아파요 (throat). For other symptoms use [thing]이/가 나요: 콧물이 나요 (runny nose), 기침이 나요 (cough), 열이 나요 (fever).

beginnerGuide.title: Want vs. must when getting medicine
beginnerGuide.body: Use V + 고 싶어요 to say what you want — 약 사고 싶어요 (I want to buy medicine). The pharmacist may tell you what you MUST do with V + 아/어야 해요 — 식후에 먹어야 해요 (you have to take it after meals). Listen for 하루에 ~번 (~ times a day) and 식후/식전 (after/before meals).

checkpoints: State at least two symptoms, e.g. 머리가 아파요 and 콧물이 나요.
Ask for directions to a pharmacy with 약국이 어디예요?
Hand over or request a prescription using 처방전 주세요.
Ask how to take the medicine with 이 약 어떻게 먹어요? and understand 하루에 세 번 / 식후에.

drills.note: Swap the part: 배가 / 목이 / 이가 아파요.
V고 싶어요 = want to. Try 쉬고 싶어요 (I want to rest).

drills.en: How do I take this medicine?
drills.note: Listen for 하루에 세 번 (3x a day) and 식후에 (after meals) in the answer.

steps: At the clinic reception, say 아파요 and answer 어디가 아파요? with [part]가/이 아파요.
Receive the 처방전 from the doctor (or skip to a pharmacy for minor symptoms).
Find a green-cross 약국 nearby; ask 약국이 어디예요? if needed.
Hand over the slip: 처방전 주세요 / 처방전 있어요.
Before leaving, ask 이 약 어떻게 먹어요? and note the timing (하루에 ~번, 식후/식전).
units.costs: A clinic visit with national health insurance is often about 5,000–15,000 KRW out of pocket; prescription medicine is usually a few thousand won. Over-the-counter cold or headache medicine at a pharmacy is typically 3,000–8,000 KRW.
units.notes: Pharmacies (약국) display a green cross. Most cold, headache, and digestive remedies are sold over the counter. Pharmacies often close in the evening and on Sundays; look for a 24-hour 약국 or a hospital pharmacy for late-night needs.

units.title: Parcels & Daily Weather
units.situation: You're expecting a 택배 (parcel) and want to know when it arrives or where it was left, and you want to check the weather and 미세먼지 (fine dust) before heading out.
units.goal: Ask whether and when a parcel has arrived, tell the courier where to leave it, and ask about today's fine dust — using 있어요/없어요 and request forms.

keyPhrases.note: 택배 = courier parcel, 왔어요 = came (past of 와요). 가 marks the subject. Very common to ask a guard or housemate.
언제 = when. Couriers often send an SMS with a rough time window. 와요 = comes.
있어요 = there is / exists. Ask the building's security desk (경비실). Opposite: 없어요 (there isn't).

keyPhrases.en: Please leave it at the door.
keyPhrases.note: 문 앞 = in front of the door, 놔 주세요 = please put/leave it. A standard delivery instruction.
경비실 = the guard/security office in an apartment building, 맡겨 주세요 = please entrust it. Common when you're out.
미세먼지 = fine dust (air pollution), 어때요? = how is it? A daily small-talk and health question in Korea.

keyPhrases.en: There's a lot of fine dust.
keyPhrases.note: 많아요 = there's a lot / it's high. On these days wear a mask (마스크). Opposite: 미세먼지가 적어요 (low).

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Hello. Is there a parcel for me?

dialogue.speaker: Guard
dialogue.en: What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Unit 504. Did a parcel come?

dialogue.speaker: Guard
dialogue.en: Yes, there's one. Here you go.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.ko: 감사합니다. 다음에는 문 앞에 놔 주세요.
dialogue.en: Thank you. Next time, please leave it at the door.

dialogue.speaker: Friend
dialogue.en: How's the fine dust today?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.ko: 미세먼지가 많아요. 마스크 쓰는 게 좋아요.
dialogue.en: There's a lot of fine dust. It's better to wear a mask.

beginnerGuide.title: 있어요 / 없어요 for parcels
beginnerGuide.body: 있어요 means 'there is / I have it' and 없어요 means 'there isn't / I don't have it.' Ask 택배 있어요? (is there a parcel?) at the security desk; the answer is 네, 있어요 or 아니요, 없어요. To ask if it arrived, use the past tense: 택배가 왔어요? (did it come?).

beginnerGuide.title: Tell the courier where to leave it
beginnerGuide.body: Most parcels are left without a signature. Tell the driver via the app or a note where to put it: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 (leave it at the door) or 경비실에 맡겨 주세요 (leave it with security). 경비실 is the staffed guard office found in most Korean apartment buildings.

beginnerGuide.title: Check fine dust like you check rain
beginnerGuide.body: 미세먼지 (fine dust, PM10/PM2.5) is part of daily life in Korea, especially in spring. People routinely ask 오늘 미세먼지 어때요? On bad days (미세먼지가 많아요) many wear a mask (마스크) outdoors. Check an air-quality app or AirKorea before going out, the same way you'd check the weather.

checkpoints: Ask whether a parcel arrived (택배가 왔어요?) and whether one is being held (택배 있어요?).
Ask when it will come with 택배 언제 와요?
Give a delivery instruction: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 or 경비실에 맡겨 주세요.
Ask and answer about fine dust with 오늘 미세먼지 어때요? / 미세먼지가 많아요.

drills.note: 있어요/없어요 to answer: 네, 왔어요 / 아니요, 안 왔어요.

drills.en: Please leave it at the door.
drills.note: Swap the place: 경비실에 / 택배함에 맡겨 주세요.

drills.en: There's a lot of fine dust.
drills.note: Opposite: 미세먼지가 적어요 (it's low). Pair with 마스크 쓰는 게 좋아요.

steps: When expecting a parcel, check your delivery SMS or app for the time window (택배 언제 와요?).
Leave an instruction for the driver: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 or 경비실에 맡겨 주세요.
If it's missing, ask the guard: 택배 있어요? / 택배가 왔어요?
Before going out, check air quality: 오늘 미세먼지 어때요?
On high-dust days (미세먼지가 많아요), wear a mask outdoors.

units.costs: Standard domestic courier (택배) shipping is typically about 3,000–5,000 KRW when you send a box; most online purchases include free or low-cost delivery. Checking weather and fine dust apps is free.
units.notes: Korean apartment deliveries are usually contactless — drivers leave parcels at the door, in a parcel box (택배함), or with the security office (경비실). Save your tracking number to follow the parcel online.
